Peter's Vision
PEE-terz VIZH-un
noun phrase (Acts 10)
From the account in Acts 10 of the sheet let down from heaven; the vision by which God prepared Peter to carry the gospel to the Gentiles.

Biblical Definition

Peter's vision is the revelation given to the apostle on the housetop at Joppa, recorded in Acts 10, by which God prepared him to receive the Gentiles into the church. As Peter prayed and grew hungry, he saw heaven opened and a great sheet let down, full of all manner of beasts, creeping things, and fowls, clean and unclean together; and a voice said, “Rise, Peter; kill, and eat.” When Peter refused, having never eaten anything common or unclean, the voice answered, “What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common,” and this was done three times. While Peter doubted what it meant, the messengers of Cornelius the Roman centurion arrived, and the Spirit bade him go with them. Peter perceived the meaning: “God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean,” and standing in the house of a Gentile he confessed, “Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons.” The dictionary holds Peter's vision to teach two truths. First, the abolition of the old ceremonial distinction between clean and unclean foods, fulfilled and set aside in Christ, who declared all meats clean. Second, and chiefly, the opening of the gospel to the Gentiles: the dividing wall is broken down, and in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek. The dictionary marks the vision against the error that would read it as a charter for moral indifference or the abolition of God's moral law; it abolished the ceremonial shadow and the partition between the nations, not the abiding commands of God. It is a landmark of redemptive history: the household of faith opened to all peoples, that the promise to Abraham might be fulfilled, in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed.

Webster 1828 Definition

The vision of the sheet let down from heaven (Acts 10), by which God abolished the clean/unclean ceremonial distinction and, chiefly, opened the gospel to the Gentiles; “What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common.”

PETER'S VISION, noun phrase. The revelation of the sheet let down from heaven at Joppa (Acts 10).

A voice said, “Rise, Peter; kill, and eat,” of beasts clean and unclean together.

“What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common” (Acts 10:15), spoken thrice.

It abolished the ceremonial distinction of clean and unclean foods, fulfilled in Christ.

Chiefly, it opened the gospel to the Gentiles: God is no respecter of persons (Acts 10:34).

Key Scripture

Ac 10:13 — "And there came a voice to him, Rise, Peter; kill, and eat."

Ac 10:15 — "And the voice spake unto him again the second time, What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common."

Ac 10:28 — "And he said unto them, Ye know how that it is an unlawful thing for a man that is a Jew to keep company, or come unto one of another nation; but God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean."

Ac 10:34 — "Then Peter opened his mouth, and said, Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons:"

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is reading the vision as a charter for moral indifference, as though “call nothing unclean” abolished God's moral law along with the ceremonial.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the careful distinction between the ceremonial law, fulfilled and set aside in Christ, and the moral law, which abides. Peter's vision is sometimes pressed into the service of moral license—“God said call nothing unclean,” therefore no behaviour may be named sin. This wrests the text. The vision abolished the dietary distinctions of the ceremonial code and broke down the partition between Jew and Gentile; it said nothing to overturn the moral commands of God, which the apostles everywhere upheld. The clean/unclean of Leviticus is fulfilled in Christ; the “thou shalt not” of the Decalogue is not.

Rightly read, Peter's vision is one of the great landmarks of redemptive history: the gospel goes to the nations, and in Christ the dividing wall between Jew and Gentile is broken down. The dictionary holds it as the fulfilment of the promise to Abraham, that in his seed all the families of the earth should be blessed. It teaches that God is no respecter of persons—not that all conduct is acceptable, but that men of every nation who fear God and work righteousness are accepted in Christ. The vision opened the church to the world; it did not open the law of God to revision.

Hebrew Roots

From the account at Joppa: the “sheet” (Greek othone) let down, the “common” (koinos) and “unclean” (akathartos) that God had cleansed (katharizo).

expand to see more

Othone, Greek, a sheet or large linen, let down from heaven in the vision.

Koinos, Greek, “common,” ceremonially defiled, what Peter would not eat.

Akathartos, Greek, unclean, the category abolished for foods in Christ.

Katharizo, Greek, to cleanse, “what God hath cleansed” (Acts 10:15).

“No respecter of persons” (Greek prosopolemptes) names God's impartiality toward the nations.

Usage

"The teacher showed that Peter's vision abolished the ceremonial law of foods, not the moral law of God."

"He preached the breaking of the wall between Jew and Gentile, the gospel opened to all nations."

"She rejoiced that God is no respecter of persons, receiving worshippers of every nation in Christ."
